claims.text: Controlled low-level oxygen addition during processing will produce an in-situ nanoscale oxide dispersion in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Controlled atmospheres during powder processing or mechanical alloying can be used to introduce the tailored oxygen content.
The resulting oxide nanoparticles will be fine and uniformly dispersed.
The oxide nanoparticles will be located at grain and phase boundaries.
Oxide nanoparticles act as sinks for radiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.
Defect trapping by oxide nanoparticles will reduce overall irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
Reduced defect accumulation will improve the radiation tolerance of the alloy.
Maintaining oxide size and volume fraction at suitable levels will avoid embrittlement and excessive phase formation.
The oxide-dispersed alloy will preserve mechanical strength and ductility under plasma-facing conditions.
After simulated fusion-relevant irradiation, the oxide-dispersed alloy will have fewer irradiation-induced defects than the unmodified baseline.
After simulated fusion-relevant irradiation, the oxide-dispersed alloy will retain hardness and tensile strength better than the unmodified baseline.
The beneficial effect should hold at low to moderate oxygen doping levels that produce nano-oxides without substantial coarsening or embrittlement.
Excess oxygen may produce detrimental oxide volume fractions and limit the beneficial effect.
Conventional refractory high-entropy alloys processed without intentional oxygen addition typically have homogeneous matrices with minimal nanoscale oxide precipitates.
A statistically significant failure to reduce defect density or retain mechanical strength relative to an identically irradiated baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
